terms.grammar: noun, third declension; feminine hospita, hospitae
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.57: alterum ad caupōnem dēvertisse, ad hospitem alterum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: One who takes a friend or a stranger under his roof for nothing; an innkeeper, caupō, is paid (Lewis & Short). The same word is the guest, and host and guest together are hospes hospitī (Cic. Deiot. 8): the sentence shows which is meant. A hostess is hospita (Cic. Verr. 2.2.24), which can also be a woman guest.

terms.gloss: host of a dinner (with or without convīviī, epulī)
terms.comment: Generally master or owner; at a dinner, the man who gives it (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: the giver of a dinner party

phrases.latin: sēdulus hospes paene macrōs ārsit dum turdōs versat in ignī
phrases.english: our attentive host nearly burnt down while turning lean thrushes over the fire

phrases.latin: cum dēfēcēre, quī modo hospes fuerat, mōnstrātor hospitiī et comes
phrases.english: when the food has run out, the man who was host a moment ago becomes guide to another welcome, and companion

phrases.latin: hic est leō hospes hominis, hic est homō medicus leōnis
phrases.english: this is the lion who was the man’s host, this is the man who was the lion’s doctor

sources: Lewis & Short: hospes · Lewis & Short: dominus · Lewis & Short: convivator
